Brainspotting is an effective psychotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) because it facilitates the completion of a process of neurophysiological reconsolidation of traumatic memory which allows full orientation to the aversively experienced event and thereby enables the brain to "reset" the memory so that it is no longer dysregulated and distressing.

Brainspotting is a form of psychotherapy which is effective for a range of disorders including post-traumatic stress disorder and other disorders in which traumatic experience has truncated adaptive orientation to the experience and its meaning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Brainspotting technique, and possibly other psychotherapies that use sustained mindful attention to traumatic memories, is based on the neurophysiological mechanism of binding together the superior colliculus and the thalamus to enable coherent thalamocorticoid processing to occur, and thereby to allow the brain to reconsolidate the memory without distress.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the Brainspot is a neuroanatomically defined point of reference which, when sustained attention is directed towards it, enables the brain's processing of traumatic memory to become coherent.
